title: French A2 Plateau: Oct 2026 Breakdown
summary: A breakdown of French A2 skills, where learners get stuck, and the hours-based plan to reach B1, refreshed for October 2026.
body_markdown:
If your french A2 speaking sounds like 'ça va, bien, et toi' on repeat, you're not alone, and you're not actually bad at French. You're sitting on roughly 1,000 word families with no reliable way to produce them in real time. That's the A2 plateau, and it has a specific shape. Let's walk through what you can already do, where you keep tripping, and the weekly plan that gets you to B1.


**TLDR:**


- French A2 means handling routine exchanges (bakery orders, directions, basic past tense) but freezing at native speed due to liaison and elision
- Your active vocabulary sits around 1,000-1,500 word families at A2, per Paul Nation's research at Victoria University of Wellington
- A2 to B1 typically takes 150-200 hours of active practice; one hour daily puts you there in 5-6 months
- The plateau breaks with pushed output under conversational pressure (Swain, 1985); more reading and passive listening keep the gap in place
- ISSEN works as the daily speaking-rep layer for A2 learners, drilling passé composé narratives and futur proche in short voice sessions


## Introduction


You passed the A2 test, or you recognize yourself in the symptoms: you can order a croissant, introduce yourself, ask where the metro is. Then a Parisian answers at full speed and your brain goes blank. That gap is the French A2 experience in one sentence.


A2 is the elementary level on the CEFR scale. You handle predictable exchanges, short descriptions, basic needs. Real conversation still slips past you.


This piece covers three things: what A2 French speakers can actually do, where learners get stuck, and the route to B1 that works, a question tied closely to[how long it takes to learn French](https://www.issen.com/blog/how-long-does-it-take-to-learn-french/) .


## What French A2 actually means


A2 is what the Council of Europe calls the[Waystage level](https://www.coe.int/en/web/common-european-framework-reference-languages/level-descriptions) : routine exchanges on familiar topics, handled slowly and predictably. In concrete French terms, you can order at a boulangerie, describe your family, book a hotel room, and follow articulated speech about things you already know.


What you cannot do yet: track native-speed conversation, defend an opinion, or narrate a messy past event with the right tenses.


A representative exchange at Gare du Nord:


- You: "Bonjour, un billet pour Lille, s'il vous plait."
- Agent: "Aller simple ou aller-retour?"


You understood the question. The follow-up about seat class lost you completely.


## The French A2 skill checklist


Tick what you can already do. Gaps become your study list.


- Use passé composé with both avoir and être in simple sentences ("j'ai mangé," "je suis allé à Lyon").
- Switch between tu and vous for a stranger, a shopkeeper, or a friend's parent.
- Understand prices and numbers up to 1,000 at moderate speed (soixante-quinze, quatre-vingt-dix included).
- Handle negation beyond ne...pas: ne...jamais, ne...plus, ne...rien, ne...personne.
- Describe your daily routine using reflexive verbs (se lever, se coucher, se brosser).
- Read a short restaurant menu or train schedule without a dictionary.
- Write a 60-word email to a landlord or host with correct greetings and sign-offs.
- Ask for directions and understand à droite, à gauche, tout droit, en face de.
- Talk about past and future weekends using passé composé and futur proche.
- Follow a slow phone call about an appointment or reservation without constant repetition.


## Typical vocabulary range at French A2


At A2, your active French vocabulary sits around 1,000 to 1,500 word families, a figure traced to Paul Nation's vocabulary research at Victoria University of Wellington.

Two categories punch above their weight. Past-tense forms (passé composé for finished actions, imparfait for background) and connector words. Learn parce que, mais, alors, donc, and puis, and your speech stops sounding like a flashcard list. "J'ai mangé au restaurant parce que j'avais faim, mais c'était trop cher" is a real A2 sentence. "J'ai mangé. C'était cher." is three disconnected ones, and connecting them is part of what makes[learning French with AI](https://www.issen.com/blog/how-to-learn-french-with-ai/) effective for A2 speakers.


## Grammar you should have locked in


Six structures you should control cold at A2. If any still require conscious thought, that's your next drill.


- Passé composé with avoir/être agreement, for finished past actions: "J'ai mangé une pomme / Elle est allée au marché."
- Imparfait, for background and habit: "Quand j'étais petit, je jouais au foot."
- Futur proche vs futur simple, for near plans versus later intentions: "Je vais partir / Je partirai."
- Reflexive verbs, for daily routine: "Je me lève à sept heures."
- Direct and indirect object pronouns (le, la, lui), to stop repeating nouns: "Je lui parle."
- Comparatives, for opinions and choices: "plus grand que, moins cher que."


## Where French A2 learners get stuck


Five plateau points keep showing up at A2, each with a specific cause and fix.


- Listening collapses at native speed. "Il y a un" lands as "ya un," "je ne sais pas" as "chaipa." Liaison and elision erase word boundaries your eyes rely on.
- Overleaning on être, avoir, and faire while richer verbs (devenir, apporter, rendre) sit unused.
- Defaulting to present to dodge the imparfait/passé composé split. "Hier je mange au restaurant" is a tell.
- Mumbling articles to hide gender guesses, so no one corrects you.
- Formulaic small talk that never escapes "ça va, bien, et toi."


The intermediate plateau is well documented, and[Swain's Output Hypothesis](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1095572.pdf) explains why: without pushed output under conversational pressure, gaps in production stay invisible.


## How to break through to French B1


A weekly plan that moves you to B1, built on four levers:


- Speaking volume. Aim for 20 to 30 minutes of spoken French, 5 days a week. A real-time voice tutor like ISSEN works as the daily rep layer. A 2024 review of[AI chatbots for speaking practice](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666920X24000316) found benefits for anxiety, confidence, and speaking outcomes.
- Targeted listening. 15 minutes a day of slightly-above-level input: InnerFrench, News in Slow French, or France Info headlines, paired with[shadowing for pronunciation](https://www.issen.com/blog/shadowing-pronunciation-technique/) if liaison and elision are still tripping you up.
- Vocabulary expansion. Pull 10 new words a day from your own conversations and review them with spaced repetition in context.
- Grammar gap closure. Pick one structure a week (subjunctive after il faut que, relative pronouns dont/où, conditional for politeness) and use it in every session until it stops feeling fragile.


## Using an AI tutor at French A2


At A2, what you lack is reps, not knowledge. A voice tutor gives you volume without the social cost of fumbling in front of a human. It also holds input in Krashen's i+1 band by adapting mid-turn and recycles the structures you missed last session, a mechanism explained in more depth in[how AI speaking practice works](https://www.issen.com/blog/how-ai-speaking-practice-works/) .


Four prompts worth running this week:


- "Raconte-moi ta journée hier." Forces passé composé across a full narrative.
- "On est au bistro, prends ma commande." Drills vous, je voudrais, and menu vocabulary.
- "Qu'est-ce que tu vas faire ce weekend?" Pushes futur proche across plans and people.
- "Décris-moi un souvenir d'enfance." Imparfait territory: habits, settings, feelings.

## Sample conversation at French A2


**At the boulangerie-café:**


- Serveur: Bonjour, qu'est-ce que je vous sers?
- Client: Bonjour, euh... je voudrais un café et un croissant, s'il vous plaît. \[1\]
- Serveur: Très bien. Sur place ou à emporter?
- Client: Sur place. Je suis arrivé en avance pour mon train. \[2\]
- Serveur: D'accord. Ça fait quatre euros cinquante.
- Client: Euh, vous acceptez la carte? \[3\]
- Serveur: Oui, bien sûr. Tapez votre code.
- Client: Merci, bonne journée!


*(English translation:)*


- Server: Hello, what can I get you?
- Customer: Hello, uh... I would like a coffee and a croissant, please.
- Server: Here or to go?
- Customer: Here. I arrived early for my train.
- Server: That's four euros fifty.
- Customer: Do you accept card?
- Server: Yes, of course. Enter your PIN.
- Customer: Thanks, have a good day!


**Notes:**


1. "Je voudrais" (conditional) is the polite A2 default; "je veux" sounds blunt to a stranger.
2. "Je suis arrivé" uses passé composé with être, required for arriver, with masculine singular agreement.
3. The "euh" hesitation marker is realistic A2 speech, buying time to assemble the next phrase.


## How long to reach French B1


To put the A2-to-B1 climb in context, the[FSI estimates 552 to 690 classroom hours](https://www.state.gov/foreign-language-training/) for professional proficiency in a Category I language like French; getting to B1 is a slice of that. These are institutional averages, not promises; your mileage depends on prior exposure, speaking volume, and how much of that time is spent producing French instead of consuming it. ## FAQ


### Am I really at A2, or lower or higher?


Signals you're still A1: you can name objects and give your age but can't form a past-tense sentence like "j'ai mangé au restaurant hier." Signals you're pushing into B1: you can argue a basic opinion and recover from a misunderstanding without switching to English.


### How do I test my French level?


Use the Council of Europe's free CEFR self-assessment grid. For a harder check, work through a past DELF A2 paper from[France Education International](https://www.france-education-international.fr/en/diplomes/delf-tout-public) .


### Can I skip straight to B1?


No. B1 descriptors assume the A2 foundation (past tenses, routine exchanges, basic connectors) is already automatic, a pattern that holds across languages, as laid out in[Spanish B1: how to get there](https://www.issen.com/blog/spanish-b1-what-you-can-say-how-to-get-there/) .


### Is French A2 enough for travel, work, or living in France?


Travel, yes. Work and residency, generally no, with most pathways expecting B1 or B2. Check service-public.fr for requirements tied to your visa status.


### What's the fastest way to leave the A2 plateau?


Speaking reps with real-time feedback. A2 learners already know more French than they can produce; forced output surfaces gaps and gets them corrected on the spot, which is the core argument for[speaking your target language from day one](https://www.issen.com/blog/speak-target-language-early-output-practice/) .


## Conclusion


A2 is a real stage of competence in its own right. You can describe your life, handle a bakery, read a menu, write a short email. The ceiling is production under pressure, and the way through comes down to speaking volume with corrective feedback.


Picture Lea, an A2 learner in Berlin moving to Lyon in four months, facing the same plateau covered in[A2 Spanish: building toward B1](https://www.issen.com/blog/a2-spanish-plateau-b1/) for learners of other languages. By the time she meets a real agent, those sentences have been rehearsed aloud a dozen times.
